---
title: "Epigenome-Wide Association Studies: a hands-on tutorial"
---

## Overview

This tutorial's intended audience is graduate students, but I hope this resource is
useful to anyone who wants to learn about array-based
DNA methylation analysis. It walks through how to process from raw Illumina IDAT
files, or a partially processed methylation dataset, to perform an Epigenome-wide 
association study (EWAS). I also include direction and resources for secondary 
analyses and annotation and interpretation of results. Everything is run on real 
data from the Grady Trauma Project; data for this project and others can be accessed
at the NCBI GEO database website. Learning objectives:

- understand what methylation data is and how it is measured with array technology
- read raw two-channel IDATs into R;
- run the quality-control checks on the raw or processed methylation data;
- know the different methods for normalization and how to do it yourself;
- learn about probe filtering, including which probes are unreliable and how ancestry-aware masks work;
- estimate blood cell composition; 
- diagnose and correct technical batch structure;
- how to create a proxy for smoking;
- fit an epigenome-wide model;
- and, annotate the top CpGs and regions.

## The dataset

The *Grady Trauma Project* (**GSE132203**) is a dataset including whole-blood Illumina
MethylationEPIC (v1, 850K) profiles from an adult cohort designed to study trauma exposure and PTSD. 
It was chosen for this tutorial because it includes important characteristics for teaching:

| Feature | Why it matters|
|---|---|
| Raw IDATs deposited | Lets us start from the true beginning, not a processed matrix. This is not always an option in reality, but it's important to understand how we get from raw data to the data used in an analysis.  |
| Deposited cell-type proportions | estimating blood cell proportions is shown in the tutorial, but this provides an opportunity to validate our findings against the original study. |
| Sentrix barcodes in filenames | the sentrix barcodes in the file names provide the technical variables chip and array position |
| Explicit age & sex, multiple exposures | The phenotypes provided in the GEO datasets are often sparse, but the Grady Trauma Project provides many of the covariates I strongly recommend to include in modeling, as well as several candidate phenotypes for association testing. |


For the purposes of the tutorial, a subset (n = 96) of the whole cohort (N = 795) is used to keep every step quick and executable with a standard laptop. The 96 samples
(12 full EPIC BeadChips × 8 positions) are balanced on PTSD status and biological sex. All 12 chips carry both PTSD cases and controls so the
phenotype is not confounded with chip. See the [Setup](00_setup.qmd) notebook
for exactly how the subset was chosen.

## How the notebooks fit together

The preprocessing-through-analysis arc maps onto these notebooks:

1. **[Setup](00_setup.qmd)** — methylation and platform background, how the data were obtained, the subset.
2. **[Quality control](01_qc.qmd)** — detection p-values, intensity, predicted sex, SNP identity.
3. **[Normalization](02_normalization.qmd)** — within- and between-array normalization.
4. **[Probe filtering](03_probe_filtering.qmd)** — problematic mapping and ancestry-aware SNP masks.
5. **[Cell composition](04_cell_composition.qmd)** — reference-based deconvolution, validated against deposited proportions.
6. **[Batch effects](05_batch_effects.qmd)** — chip/position diagnosis; decide whether and how to correct.
7. **[EWAS](06_ewas.qmd)** — basic single site association testing with R.
8. **[Snakemake pipeline](07_pipeline.qmd)** — the same analysis as a versioned, one-command reproducible workflow.
9. **[Annotation](08_annotation.qmd)** — mapping top CpGs to genes, regions (DMRs), and regulatory context.

Each notebook loads the object saved by the previous one, so you can work
through them in order or jump to any step and pick up the saved checkpoint.
